title: Pressure-cooker leek risotto
subtitle: A silky, vegetarian risotto without the stirring
excerpt: Leeks and arborio rice cooked under pressure in vegetable stock. The leeks soften into the rice during the cook and finish with cold butter and Parmesan into a deeply creamy result.
sourceNotes: Leek risotto is a northern Italian winter variation on the classic risotto template, leeks replace onion as the allium base and soften into the rice during cooking. The pressure cooker method is an adaptation of traditional riso al porro documented in Italian home-cooking literature.

recipe.makeAheadNotes: Risotto does not hold well, make and serve in one go.

content.text: Leek risotto is a winter dish. Slice the leeks thinly and cook them until soft before the rice goes in. They almost dissolve into the finished dish. Eight minutes at high pressure produces a creamy result. Finish with cold butter and Parmesan stirred vigorously off the heat.

The leeks serve as both the aromatic base and a vegetable element in the finished dish, unlike onion-based risotto, where the base is a background flavour, here the leek is a presence throughout. Use only the white and pale green parts; the tough dark green tops can go into stock.
Serve in warm bowls immediately after finishing. Risotto waits for no one, the starch continues to absorb liquid and the texture changes within minutes of leaving the pot.

items.prepNote: white and pale green parts only, thinly sliced

content.text: Set the pressure cooker to sauté or use the open pot on the hob. Heat {{olive-oil}} of olive oil over medium heat. Add the leeks and garlic. Cook, stirring occasionally, for 8 minutes until the leeks have softened and reduced significantly in volume. They should be completely limp and starting to turn pale gold at the edges.

Add {{arborio-rice}} of arborio rice and stir for 1 minute. Pour in the hot vegetable stock. Season with salt and pepper. Seal the lid and bring to high pressure. Cook at high pressure for 8 minutes, then quick-release.
Open the lid. Add the cold butter and Parmesan and stir vigorously for 1 to 2 minutes until creamy and cohesive. Taste and adjust the seasoning. Serve straight away in warm bowls.

rows.cause: The rice absorbed all the liquid and continued to swell after opening.
rows.fix: Stir in a splash of hot stock or boiling water to loosen. Add it a little at a time and stir through.

rows.symptom: The leeks are stringy in the finished dish
rows.cause: The dark green tops were included, or the leeks were not cooked long enough before the rice went in.
rows.fix: Use only the white and pale green parts of the leek. Give them the full 8 minutes of sautéing, they should be completely soft before the rice is added.

rows.symptom: The risotto is not creamy despite adding butter and Parmesan
rows.cause: The butter and cheese were added to a very hot pot, causing the fat to separate rather than emulsify.
rows.fix: Let the risotto cool for 1 minute before adding butter. Stir vigorously and continuously for at least 2 minutes, the cream comes from the mechanical action as much as the ingredients.

content.text: Leek risotto is cold-weather food. It suits a quiet weeknight in January when the garden looks brown and the kitchen needs to warm up. It is also truly meatless in a way that does not feel apologetic, the leeks have enough flavour and substance to carry the dish on their own.
